title: The Byzantine churches
hookLine: Ukrainian, Melkite, Ruthenian, Romanian and more pray in the Byzantine tradition

cards: Watch the hand. The thumb and the first two fingers press together at the tips. The last two fold down into the palm.
Then the hand goes to the forehead, to the chest, to the right shoulder, and then the left. A Latin Catholic touches the left shoulder first.
Three fingers joined, they say, for the Trinity; two folded, for the two natures of Christ, God and man. It's a small thing, a sign of the cross going the other way.
And that hand belongs to a Catholic, praying in a tradition with long habits of its own.

teach.h: BYZANTIUM: A CITY, THEN A TRADITION.
teach.b: First, the name. Byzantine comes from Byzantium, the old name of the city later called Constantinople.

The way of worship that grew up there, its liturgy, chant, icons and calendar of feasts, carried the city's name with it, and the Catechism lists the Byzantine among the Church's great liturgical traditions.

Several Eastern Catholic churches pray in this tradition, each its own church sui iuris: Ukrainian Greek Catholics; Melkites, whose home is in Syria, Lebanon and the Holy Land, and who pray in Arabic and Greek; Ruthenians, from the Carpathian mountains; Romanian Greek Catholics; and others.
Different languages, different histories, the same shape of prayer. Third, the neighbors.

The Byzantine Catholic liturgy is, for the most part, the liturgy of the Orthodox churches: the same prayers, the same icons, often the same music. The difference isn't in the incense; it's in communion.
Byzantine Catholics are in full communion with the bishop of Rome, and name the pope in their prayers.

teach.h: CLOSE TO THE ORTHODOX, IN COMMUNION.
teach.b: They stand close to their Orthodox neighbors and close to Rome at the same time, and that place in between hasn't always been an easy one to hold. Fourth, the open door.
The Church's law says a Catholic keeps the Sunday obligation by attending Mass in any Catholic rite.

teach.h: ANY CATHOLIC IS WELCOME ON SUNDAY.
teach.b: So a Latin Catholic can walk into a Byzantine Catholic church on Sunday, stand through a liturgy in another shape, receive communion from a spoon, and be welcome.

how: Byzantine Catholics celebrate the Divine Liturgy, sung throughout, with icons and incense; they make the sign of the cross from the right shoulder to the left, and Latin Catholics may attend and receive communion there.

games.q: you're a Latin Catholic visiting a Byzantine Catholic church on Sunday. the liturgy is sung, there's an icon wall, and communion is given from a spoon. what do you do?
o: leave, because this isn't your Mass.
stay, pray with them, and come forward for communion.
stay, but treat it as watching someone else's church.
games.why: it's a Catholic liturgy, and the Church's law counts it for the Sunday obligation. same Church, different room.

practice: If you like, make the sign of the cross their way, three fingers joined, two folded, forehead, chest, right shoulder, then left, and notice your hand doing something familiar a new way.
Then hold them in mind: Ukrainians, Melkites, Ruthenians, Romanians, at home and far from home.
If you pray, use a prayer sung in their liturgy, Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us; if not, simply hold them with good will.

wordCard.voice: The Byzantine churches. Eastern Catholic churches praying in the tradition of Constantinople, sharing worship with the Orthodox, in communion with Rome. Today's word.
